content.text:
I reviewed the 29 open issues and read through the three sessions from Sep 9–10 (~12.5 MB of transcript covering #97, #99, #100, #101). Here's what the logs actually show, and what I'd do about it.

## What the sessions cost you

Command counts across the two deploy sessions:

| | count |
|---|---|
| `gcloud compute ssh` (into the VM to fix things by hand) | 53 |
| local `docker`/`podman` (repro containers) | 77 |
| `pulumi preview` / `pulumi up` | 29 / 28 |
| `just ci` / `just check` (14 of them failing) | 37 / 34 |
| `pulumi cancel` (stack left locked by a killed run) | 2 |

And the recurring failures:

- **14×** `invocation of gcp:organizations/getClientConfig returned an error: Error setting access_token: oauth2:` — expired ADC
- **3×** `Reauthentication failed. cannot prompt during non-interactive execution`
- **~10 distinct** IAM 403s mid-apply (`secretmanager.secrets.create`, `iam.serviceAccounts.getIamPolicy`, `artifactregistry.repositories.getIamPolicy`), plus 3 `gcloud config set account` switches
- **9×** `Directus at https://… did not become reachable within 180000ms`
- **1×** `--yes or --skip-preview must be passed in to proceed when running in non-interactive mode` → `just deploy` abandoned in favor of a hand-rolled `export DOCKER_HOST=…; pulumi up --cwd …`

## Five root causes

**1. Changing an app requires replacing the VM — or SSHing in.** This is the big one, and it explains the 53 SSH calls. The whole compose stack is embedded in cloud-init `user-data` (`substrate-bootstrap.ts:38`), and COS runs cloud-init **only on first boot** — `compute.ts:74` says so in a comment. So editing `docker-compose.yml` produces a Pulumi diff that changes nothing live. Your only options are hand-apply over SSH, or force a VM replace, which with `deleteBeforeReplace` means downtime *and* races the Directus dynamic resources against their 180s reachability window. That's cause #4 too.

**2. ADC expiry fails the program before it can even diff.** `gcp.organizations.getClientConfig({})` is called at **module scope** in `substrate.ts:52` and `run-reports-job.ts:42`. It runs on every `preview` and every `up`, so a stale token doesn't fail one resource — it kills the whole run with an opaque `oauth2:` error. Combined with `gcloud`'s inability to reprompt in a non-interactive shell, this is a hard stop that needs you at the keyboard.

**3. `ungood@` genuinely can't deploy the platform.** `config.ts:14` grants deploy rights per-user, and those rights (`run.developer` + `artifactregistry.writer` + impersonation) predate the platform work. Every new resource class hits a fresh 403, and the workaround is switching to `master@` — exactly what your own access policy in CLAUDE.md prohibits. This is #87, already written up correctly.

**4. Infra and app-config live in one stack with a boot-time dependency.** `people-hub.ts` creates Directus schema/roles/users by HTTP against a VM that the same `pulumi up` is still booting. `docs/manual-setup.md` §6.2 already concedes "on a truly fresh deploy this is often the *second* `pulumi up`."

**5. No CI beyond `just ci`.** No `pulumi preview` on PRs, no `.github/dependabot.yml` (#63 is still open). Infra correctness is only ever discovered at apply time, against production, by you.

---

## The plan

### Tier 1 — cheap, do first (half a day, high relief)

| # | Change | Fixes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `just doctor` — one preflight that checks devshell, active account, ADC validity *and identity*, pulumi login, podman socket; prints the exact fix command for whatever's wrong. Make `deploy` and `preview` depend on it. | 2, 3 |
| 2 | Move both `getClientConfig` calls inside their `docker.Image` resource so an expired token fails one resource with a clear message, not the whole program. | 2 |
| 3 | `just preview` and `just deploy yes=""` — pass `--yes` through so it works non-interactively; stop the hand-rolled `DOCKER_HOST` incantation. Add `just ssh` and `just logs <service>` (you typed that IAP command 53 times). | agent friction |
| 4 | Fix the README/CLAUDE.md auth table. It says Pulumi uses your `gcloud auth login` session. **It uses ADC.** This wrong doc is the direct cause of the "deploy 403 after `just auth-adc`" class of failure in #83. | 3 |
| 5 | Split `just fmt` (writes) from `just check` (CI, `--fail-on-change`). 14 of 34 `check` runs failed on formatting alone. | churn |
| 6 | Add `.github/dependabot.yml` (npm + github-actions, weekly, grouped). Closes half of #63. | 5 |

### Tier 2 — the real fix (1–2 days, biggest payoff)

**7. Make the substrate bootstrap re-runnable, and let `pulumi up` apply it.**

Convert `bootstrapScript` into an idempotent script installed as a systemd unit, and have Pulumi push+run it via `@pulumi/command`'s `remote.Command` (or a `local.Command` wrapping `gcloud compute ssh --tunnel-through-iap`, which needs no new IAM — `compute.ts:35` already grants `iap.tunnelResourceAccessor` + `compute.osLogin`), with `triggers: [hash(composeContent), imageUrl]`.

Result: editing `docker-compose.yml` becomes one `pulumi up` with no VM replace, no downtime, no SSH. This collapses the loop that consumed most of last night.

Worth flagging explicitly, since you rejected it once: this gives `pulumi up` shell-exec on the VM, which you turned down for #99. That was the right call there — building SSH machinery to self-heal a one-off bootstrap bug. This is different: it's the *normal* deploy path for every app change from here forward, and it's the thing that makes FreeScout (#67) and Listmonk (#71) deployable at all without a VM rebuild each time.

**8. Automate the Postgres `GRANT` (manual-setup.md §6.1) on top of #7.** The VM has a network path to Cloud SQL's private IP; once remote-exec exists, this stops being irreducible. Removes the last hand-step from a fresh environment build.

**9. Ship #87 — `it-admin@` Google Group + a custom `platformDeployer` role**, and change `config.ts`'s `deployers` from `user:` to `group:`. This is what ends the `master@`/`ungood@` switching, and it's also your onboarding story: adding dev #2 becomes "add them to the group," not a PR against `config.ts` plus a deploy.

**10. Ship #83's project-local credentials** — `CLOUDSDK_CONFIG="$PWD/.gcloud"` in `.envrc` (gitignored). The flake already sets `CLOUDSDK_ACTIVE_CONFIG_NAME`, but ADC is still the one global file, so personal and CSC credentials collide. Small change, removes a whole category of confusion. Default ADC to *you*; impersonate `report-runner@` per-invocation only.

### Tier 3 — for the second dev (a day, after Tier 2)

**11. `pulumi preview` on PRs** via Workload Identity Federation (no key files) posting the diff as a PR comment. Keep **apply human-gated from a laptop** — consistent with the #64 decision. This is the single guardrail that makes it safe for someone else to touch `packages/infrastructure`.

**12. `just dev-up` — local compose parity.** The one thing that went *well* last night was reproducing Directus locally in Docker to prove the 401 hypothesis. Make that a first-class recipe (Postgres + Directus + Caddy from the same committed compose file) so app-layer work never needs the live VM. This is the cheap alternative to a dev GCP project.

**13. `docs/onboarding.md`** — one linear day-one path: `direnv allow` → `just doctor` → join `it-admin@` → `just dev-up`. Then trim `manual-setup.md` to genuinely-manual steps only, and pin the Directus version in one place with a CI check (the drift that caused #101).

## What I'd skip

- **A separate dev/staging GCP project.** Doubles the ~$63/mo and the surface area. `just dev-up` (#12) covers 90% of it.
- **Atlantis/GitOps/auto-apply from CI.** Preview-in-CI, apply-from-laptop is the right ratio for one dev.
- **Self-healing deploy automation.** You already called this correctly on #99.
- **Monitoring/alerting build-out.** That's #66 and it's a real epic; don't fold it into a tooling pass.

---

Rough sequencing: Tier 1 is one session. Tier 2 items 7+8 are one focused PR, 9+10 another. Tier 3 after.

Want me to file these as GitHub issues (Tier 1 as one issue with a checklist, Tier 2/3 as individual ones cross-linked to #83/#87/#21/#63)? I'd also close #21 into #83, since #83 supersedes it.

message.content: One thing before we create the issues. Would it make sense to split the one pulumi stack into multiple? Maybe an "infrastructure" that is the minimum set of resources to enable individual developers (in it-admin) to do development - it would contain only the resources needed to be deployed by master@ and should change rarely. Then "substrate" which would be resources shared by multiple apps. Then a stack for each app?

content.thinking:
I want to give an opinionated answer grounded in the actual code, so I'm examining the dependency graph in packages/infrastructure/src to find the natural seams and understand what splitting into bootstrap/substrate/app-per-stack would cost versus gain, keeping Pulumi's stack terminology in mind.

A "stack" is really an instance of a "project" — what the user's describing is actually multiple projects with cross-project StackReferences, since Pulumi.yaml is per-project and `pulumi up` runs one project at a time; that distinction matters and is worth clarifying. The bootstrap/foundation split is genuinely valuable because it maps to a different actor, cadence, and permission set (master@ rarely, it-admin routinely) — that's the real justification, not stack size. For per-app stacks, I'm weighing benefits like reduced blast radius, independent applies, faster previews, and natural resolution of app-layer/boot-time coupling, against costs like StackReference plumbing, manual ordering or a `just deploy-all` command, and secrets/IAM grants that cross stack boundaries.

The hardest problem is that the compose file is a single monolithic file on one VM shared by all apps — if each app becomes its own stack, ownership of docker-compose.yml gets murky, and I think this needs to lead the discussion. Since `docker compose` supports multiple files and Caddy supports importing config fragments, splitting is feasible if each app stack drops its own compose and Caddyfile fragments onto the VM and runs its own `docker compose up -d` project — though I'm also considering a cleaner variant where each app becomes its own separate compose project entirely.

That approach avoids file merging and cross-stack conflicts, but ironically resembles the exact cause of issue #99, where a stale second compose project collided on ports 80/443. The fix here is that only substrate's project should bind host ports, while app projects connect over the shared network without binding anything — making port ownership unambiguous and multi-project setups safe. I need to verify the actual compose file and Caddyfile to confirm, and this whole approach depends heavily on having a re-runnable bootstrap so app stacks can be reapplied cleanly.

I want to check if the codebase already treats apps as "slices" — looking at portal.ts and directus.ts to see if that mental model already exists, since splitting into separate projects would just formalize an existing boundary. I should also think about cost implications, like whether Pulumi Cloud has a viable free tier for individual use.

I see it's using Pulumi Cloud as the backend given the app.pulumi.com URL — I'll flag that as something to verify rather than assert. Let me go look at the actual files now.

content.content:
# The substrate VM's whole compose stack: every surface behind the one shared Caddy container,
# routed by hostname. Today that's the cycsail.team portal (gated by oauth2-proxy) and the people
# hub (Directus, its own native Google OIDC login — no oauth2-proxy needed for that surface). Secret
# values come from an env file written at boot from Secret Manager (see cloud-init in
# infrastructure/src/substrate-bootstrap.ts) — nothing sensitive lives in git.
services:
  caddy:
    image: ${CADDY_IMAGE}
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      SITE_DOMAIN: ${SITE_DOMAIN}
      DIRECTUS_DOMAIN: ${DIRECTUS_DOMAIN}
    ports:
      - "80:80"
      - "443:443"
    volumes:
      - caddy_data:/data
      - caddy_config:/config
    depends_on:
      - oauth2-proxy
      - directus

  oauth2-proxy:
    image: quay.io/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy:v7.6.0
    restart: unless-stopped
    command:
      - --http-address=0.0.0.0:4180
      - --reverse-proxy=true
      # Auth-only in front of Caddy: oauth2-proxy makes the allow/deny decision; Caddy serves.
      - --upstream=static://202
      - --provider=google
      - --redirect-url=https://${SITE_DOMAIN}/oauth2/callback
      - --cookie-domain=${SITE_DOMAIN}
      - --whitelist-domain=${SITE_DOMAIN}
      # Accept any Google account (personal Gmail included); the group check below is the real gate.
      - --email-domain=*
      # Authorization = membership in the all@ group (which nests staff@, volunteers@, …).
      - --google-group=${OAUTH2_PROXY_GOOGLE_GROUP}
      - --google-admin-email=${OAUTH2_PROXY_GOOGLE_ADMIN_EMAIL}
      # Use the VM's own service account (Application Default Credentials via the metadata server)
      # for the Directory API group lookup — no long-lived key file. The substrate SA must have
      # domain-wide delegation for admin.directory.group.readonly (see ../README.md).
      - --google-use-application-default-credentials=true
      - --set-xauthrequest=true
    environment:
      # Shared platform-wide Google OAuth client (substrate.ts) — SSO between this and Directus.
      OAUTH2_PROXY_CLIENT_ID: ${GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID}
      OAUTH2_PROXY_CLIENT_SECRET: ${GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET}
      OAUTH2_PROXY_COOKIE_SECRET: ${OAUTH2_PROXY_COOKIE_SECRET}

  # The people hub. Talks to its own database on the shared Cloud SQL instance over private IP
  # (no Cloud SQL Auth Proxy needed — the VM and Cloud SQL are on the same VPC).
  #
  # Directus 12+ (MSCL-licensed) gates custom/relational permission rules (the $CURRENT_USER-scoped
  # filters the Guardian policy depends on — see docs/people-hub-schema.md) behind a license; CYC
  # has one via Directus's Open Innovation Grant (nonprofit, well under the $5M revenue / 50
  # employee thresholds — see docs/manual-setup.md §6). LICENSE_KEY below is required for the
  # Guardian role to actually work, not just for this version number.
  directus:
    image: directus/directus:12.3.1
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      KEY: ${DIRECTUS_KEY}
      SECRET: ${DIRECTUS_SECRET}
      LICENSE_KEY: ${DIRECTUS_LICENSE_KEY}
      DB_CLIENT: pg
      DB_HOST: ${DIRECTUS_DB_HOST}
      DB_PORT: "5432"
      DB_DATABASE: directus
      DB_USER: directus
      DB_PASSWORD: ${DIRECTUS_DB_PASSWORD}
      ADMIN_EMAIL: ${DIRECTUS_ADMIN_EMAIL}
      ADMIN_PASSWORD: ${DIRECTUS_ADMIN_PASSWORD}
      PUBLIC_URL: https://${DIRECTUS_DOMAIN}
      # Native Google OIDC, same shared client as oauth2-proxy above — see
      # docs/manual-setup.md for the one-time OAuth client setup. No oauth2-proxy in front of this
      # surface; Directus enforces its own login + roles.
      AUTH_PROVIDERS: google
      AUTH_GOOGLE_DRIVER: openid
      AUTH_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID: ${GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID}
      AUTH_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET: ${GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET}
      AUTH_GOOGLE_ISSUER_URL: https://accounts.google.com
      AUTH_GOOGLE_IDENTIFIER_KEY: email
      AUTH_GOOGLE_ALLOW_PUBLIC_REGISTRATION: "false"

volumes:
  caddy_data:
  caddy_config:
=== Caddyfile ===
# Caddy config for the substrate VM: the single public listener fronting every surface, routed by
# hostname.
#
# cycsail.team (SITE_DOMAIN): every request is gated by oauth2-proxy (Google), restricted to
# members of the all@ group, so reaching the static files at all IS the authorization check — the
# portal itself is a purely static site with no backend.
#
# directus.* (DIRECTUS_DOMAIN): the people hub's data layer (Directus itself — an admin screen, not
# customer-facing). No oauth2-proxy gate here — Directus authenticates via its own native Google
# OIDC and enforces its own roles/permissions server-side, so this is a plain reverse proxy.
#
# Both domains are provided by the compose environment so the same image works for any domain.

{$DIRECTUS_DOMAIN} {
	reverse_proxy directus:8055
}

{$SITE_DOMAIN} {
	# oauth2-proxy's own endpoints (sign-in, callback, sign-out) must be reachable unauthenticated.
	handle /oauth2/* {
		reverse_proxy oauth2-proxy:4180
	}

	handle {
		# Ask oauth2-proxy whether this request is authenticated + authorized (member of all@).
		forward_auth oauth2-proxy:4180 {
			uri /oauth2/auth
			# Pass the resolved identity through to responses (not used by the static site today,
			# but makes the signed-in user visible for debugging / future use).
			copy_headers X-Auth-Request-Email X-Auth-Request-User

			# On a 401 from oauth2-proxy, send the browser to the Google sign-in flow.
			@unauthorized status 401
			handle_response @unauthorized {
				redir * /oauth2/sign_in?rd={http.request.uri}
			}
		}

		root * /srv
		file_server
	}
}

    image: directus/directus:12.3.1
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:

      SECRET: ${DIRECTUS_SECRET}
      LICENSE_KEY: ${DIRECTUS_LICENSE_KEY}
      DB_CLIENT: pg
      DB_HOST: ${DIRECTUS_DB_HOST}
      DB_PORT: "5432"
      DB_DATABASE: directus

      ADMIN_EMAIL: ${DIRECTUS_ADMIN_EMAIL}

=== Caddyfile ===
# Caddy config for the substrate VM: the single public listener fronting every surface, routed by
# hostname.
#
# cycsail.team (SITE_DOMAIN): every request is gated by oauth2-proxy (Google), restricted to
# members of the all@ group, so reaching the static files at all IS the authorization check — the
# portal itself is a purely static site with no backend.
#
# directus.* (DIRECTUS_DOMAIN): the people hub's data layer (Directus itself — an admin screen, not
# customer-facing). No oauth2-proxy gate here — Directus authenticates via its own native Google
# OIDC and enforces its own roles/permissions server-side, so this is a plain reverse proxy.
#
# Both domains are provided by the compose environment so the same image works for any domain.

{$DIRECTUS_DOMAIN} {
	reverse_proxy directus:8055
}

{$SITE_DOMAIN} {
	# oauth2-proxy's own endpoints (sign-in, callback, sign-out) must be reachable unauthenticated.
	handle /oauth2/* {
		reverse_proxy oauth2-proxy:4180
	}

	handle {
		# Ask oauth2-proxy whether this request is authenticated + authorized (member of all@).
		forward_auth oauth2-proxy:4180 {
			uri /oauth2/auth
			# Pass the resolved identity through to responses (not used by the static site today,
			# but makes the signed-in user visible for debugging / future use).
			copy_headers X-Auth-Request-Email X-Auth-Request-User

			# On a 401 from oauth2-proxy, send the browser to the Google sign-in flow.
			@unauthorized status 401
			handle_response @unauthorized {
				redir * /oauth2/sign_in?rd={http.request.uri}
			}
		}

		root * /srv
		file_server
	}
}

content.text:
Yes — and one of the three splits you're describing is the fix for the exact thing that forced you into `master@` last night. But I'd draw the boundaries a bit differently than "infrastructure / substrate / app," and I'd make `foundation` much smaller than you're imagining.

First, terminology, because it changes the file layout: what you want is multiple Pulumi **projects** (each with one `prod` stack), not multiple stacks of one project. Multiple stacks of the same project means environments (prod/dev). So: three `Pulumi.yaml`s, wired with `StackReference`.

## The boundary rule

A project boundary earns its keep when it separates a **different actor × different cadence × different permission set**. Size and tidiness aren't reasons. By that test:

| Project | Contents | Who applies | Cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| `access` | The custom `platformDeployer` role, project-level IAM bound to `it-admin@`, org policy, break-glass grants | `master@` only | ~never |
| `substrate` | network + private services connection, Cloud SQL **instance**, the VM + `substrate-runner` SA + IAP grants, static IP, DNS zones, artifact registry, shared Google OAuth client secrets, Caddy image, **the only containers binding :80/:443**, the portal (static site) | `it-admin` | occasionally |
| `people-hub` | its Postgres database + role, its secrets, `directus.cycsail.team` A record, the Directus compose project, schema/roles/users | `it-admin` | constantly |

Note what I did to your first stack: it's not "the minimum infrastructure," it's **access control only** — roughly 30 lines. That's the strongest version of the idea. The reason you had to be `master@` isn't that networks and databases are special; it's that `ungood@` can't grant `ungood@` the role `ungood@` needs. That chicken-and-egg is the *entire* content of the boundary. Everything else in your "infrastructure" tier (VPC, Cloud SQL, DNS) needs no super-admin once `platformDeployer` exists — so putting it in the rare-change stack would just make the rare-change stack change often.

This also means `access` ships **with** #87, not as separate work. Same problem, same PR.

## Per-app splits: yes, but they force a compose-model change

This is the real work, and it's why you asked at the right moment.

Today `packages/substrate/deploy/docker-compose.yml` is one file containing caddy + oauth2-proxy + directus, embedded into `user-data` as one compose project named `substrate`. If `people-hub` becomes its own project, it cannot own a slice of a file that the `substrate` project writes — two Pulumi programs writing one file is a conflict Pulumi has no way to merge.

The model that makes it work: **one compose project per app on the VM.**

- `substrate` creates an external docker network and runs caddy + oauth2-proxy. Caddy gets `import /etc/caddy/conf.d/*.caddy`. **Only substrate binds host ports.**
- each app stack ships its own `deploy/docker-compose.yml`, brings it up as its own project (`docker compose -p people-hub up -d`) attached to that network, binds **no** host ports, drops `conf.d/people-hub.caddy`, and reloads Caddy.

I know how that reads given #99, whose root cause was a stale second compose project fighting for :80/:443. That's an argument for one specific rule, not against the model: with host ports owned exclusively by substrate, that entire failure class is gone — apps are reachable over the shared network, so there's nothing to collide on.

Two things fall out for free:

- **Root cause #4 dissolves.** The 9× "Directus did not become reachable within 180000ms" happens because schema resources race a VM this same `pulumi up` is booting. In the split, the people-hub program starts the Directus container *and then* waits for it, in one program, after substrate is already up. `manual-setup.md`'s "on a truly fresh deploy this is often the second `pulumi up`" becomes `just deploy` running three projects in order.
- **Previews get much faster and much narrower.** You ran 29 of them.

## Where I'd stop splitting

An app earns a project when it has its **own database, own schema/state, own lifecycle**. Directus/people-hub qualifies; FreeScout (#67) and Listmonk (#71) will.

The portal does not — `portal.ts` is 25 lines: a cookie secret and an A record for a static site Caddy already serves. Keep it in `substrate`. Same logic says the link shortener (#73) probably never earns one either.

`run-reports-job` is the odd one: zero substrate coupling, own SA, own secrets, cron lifecycle. It's cheap to give it its own `reports` project and equally fine to leave it. I'd leave it in `substrate` for now and split it the day it annoys you.

So: **three projects, not five-plus.**

## The migration, and the one genuinely dangerous part

Splitting a live stack means moving resources between state files, and `database.ts` has `deletionProtection: true` on an instance holding data you can't recreate. A botched move is the worst outcome in this entire plan. The path that avoids most of it:

1. **Don't migrate the big stuff at all.** Rename the existing `infrastructure` project to `substrate` and leave the network, Cloud SQL, VM, static IP, and DNS zones exactly where they sit. Zero state movement for everything expensive.
2. **Create `access` fresh.** Its contents are almost all *new* resources (custom role, group bindings). Nothing to move.
3. **Carve out `people-hub`.** This is the only real migration, and it's the cheap end: a database, a role, four secrets, an A record, and the Directus dynamic resources — which you'd want recreated anyway.

For step 3, use `pulumi state move` if your CLI version has it, otherwise export/edit/import. Either way: **export the Directus database first**, and run `--target`ed previews and read every diff before applying. If a preview proposes deleting a `gcp:sql` resource, stop.

## What this does to the sequencing

One important consequence: **the per-app split is only possible after Tier 2 item #7 (re-runnable bootstrap), and #7's design depends on knowing the split is coming.** Built as "re-render the one monolithic compose file and restart," it would have to be redone. Built as "each stack pushes its own compose project and Caddy fragment, then reloads," the split is nearly free afterward.

So the revised order:

- **Tier 1** unchanged (preflight, lazy `getClientConfig`, docs, `just fmt`, dependabot).
- **Tier 2a:** `access` project + custom `platformDeployer` role + `it-admin@` group — was #87/#9. Do this first; it's what stops the `master@` dance, and it's nearly migration-free.
- **Tier 2b:** #7, **designed for per-app compose projects.** Caddy `conf.d` imports, shared external network, port ownership rule.
- **Tier 2c:** carve out `people-hub`. Automates the §6.1 `GRANT` on the way (#8) since the app stack now has remote-exec on a VM with a network path to Cloud SQL.
- **Tier 3** unchanged, and item #11 (`pulumi preview` on PRs) gets better here — three narrow previews instead of one that touches everything.

Honest cost: 8–12 StackReference outputs to plumb (put a typed `refs.ts` in each project so app code never sprinkles string-keyed `getOutput` calls), `enableService` duplicated per program (harmless — `disableOnDestroy: false` already makes it idempotent), and three applies wrapped in `just deploy`. `Secret.grant()` survives unchanged, incidentally — the grantee is just a member string, so an app stack granting the substrate SA read on its own secret works identically across a boundary. Worth confirming your Pulumi Cloud plan doesn't bill per stack; if it does, the GCS backend is free.

Want me to fold this into the issue set — `access`, the compose-model change, and the `people-hub` carve-out as three issues under a "split the Pulumi program" epic, with the migration safety notes in the carve-out issue?

content.text:
Both changes make sense, and moving Directus into `substrate` is the more consequential one — it turns Directus into a shared service like Cloud SQL and Caddy, and app projects become pure Directus configuration. That's coherent, and it matches what you were circling in the finance-app conversation: one instance, many app schemas sharing the program/session/class vocabulary.

But it surfaces a hazard I need to raise before this becomes issues.

## Whole-snapshot schema apply is destructive across apps

`applySchema` (`directus-client.ts:88`) posts the **entire** schema snapshot to `/schema/diff`. Directus's diff compares your snapshot against the whole instance and returns everything needed to make the instance match — including **deletions for collections your snapshot doesn't mention**.

So with one instance and two app projects: `people-hub` applies its snapshot, and the diff proposes dropping every `finance` collection. Then `finance` applies and drops people-hub's. Each `pulumi up` silently destroys the other app's schema and data. Today you have exactly one app schema, so this has never bitten — it becomes live the moment there's a second.

Worth confirming against a throwaway `directus/directus:12.3.1` container before building anything on it (same repro you already used for #99: create two collections, snapshot only one, diff, look for a `delete` in the response). I'm fairly confident that's the behavior, but it's cheap to verify and it's load-bearing for the whole design.

**The fix, cheap version:** scope the diff. Each app's `DirectusSchema` reads the live snapshot (`GET /schema/snapshot`), replaces only its own collections with the ones from its `schema.yaml`, and diffs *that* merged snapshot. Other apps' collections match, so nothing gets deleted; within the app's own namespace, deletions still work correctly.

The safety of that depends on the app's owned-collection list being accurate — a forgotten collection gets dropped. So **derive it from `schema.yaml` itself**, never a hand-maintained parallel list. Bonus: `people-hub.ts:allCollections` is exactly such a parallel list today (used for the Staff permission rules) and can be derived the same way, killing the duplication.

**The correct-long-term version:** stop using snapshot apply. Fan `schema.yaml` out into per-collection `DirectusCollection`/`DirectusField`/`DirectusRelation` dynamic resources against `/collections`, `/fields`, `/relations`. Cross-app deletion becomes impossible by construction, and you get real Pulumi semantics — a renamed field shows as a replace, previews show actual diffs, instead of the whole schema being one opaque resource. You already have the pattern (`directus.ts`) and a testable client, so it's more typing than difficulty.

My recommendation: **scoped diff now** (small, reuses everything, keeps the reviewable committed snapshot), **fan-out when the second app schema actually lands**. Put a comment at `applySchema` saying why, so future-you doesn't add app #2 on top of the unsafe version.

## Where roles, users, and permissions land

This splits along a natural seam, and the existing code already has the right shapes:

- **`substrate`** owns `DirectusRole` (Staff/Coach/Guardian) and `DirectusUser`. Roles are identity concepts that map to your Google Groups and span apps — a Staff member needs both the people hub and the finance app. Users obviously span apps.
- **each app** owns its `DirectusPermissionRule`s, which reference its own collections and attach them to role IDs read from the StackReference.

That requires one modest refactor: `DirectusPermissionRule` is currently an interface passed *into* `DirectusRole` as `permissionRules`. It becomes its own dynamic resource keyed by (roleId, collection, action), so an app can add rules to a role it doesn't own.

Deploying this project as yourself doesn't work, and the local tooling doesn't tell you why.

- 14 × `invocation of gcp:organizations/getClientConfig returned an error: Error setting
  access_token: oauth2:` — expired ADC. `getClientConfig({})` is called at **module scope**

  can even produce a diff, with an error that doesn't say "re-auth".

tables in `README.md:48` and CLAUDE.md say `pulumi` and `docker` use your `gcloud auth login`
session. They use **ADC**. That's the direct cause of the "deploy 403 because ADC was impersonating
`report-runner@`" failure recorded in #83.

One change, in two parts: the IAM that makes a non-super-admin deploy possible, and the local
tooling that makes it obvious when your credentials are wrong.

### 1. New `access` Pulumi project — identities and project-scoped IAM

A separate project (not stack — its own `Pulumi.yaml`), applied by `master@` and changing rarely.
It owns everything a deployer must not be able to grant itself:

- A custom **`deployer`** role, scoped to what `pulumi up` actually needs (derived from the denials

  `cloudsql`, `dns`, `servicenetworking`, `run`, `artifactregistry`, `secretmanager`. Deliberately
  **not** `resourcemanager.projectIamAdmin` — see below.
- The `it-admin@cyccommunitysailing.org` group bound to `deployer`, plus break-glass grants for
  `master@` (and `commander@` when #81 lands).
- **All service accounts** (`substrate-runner`, `report-runner`), exported for other projects.
- **Every `gcp.projects.IAMMember`** — the SA `logging.logWriter`/`monitoring.metricWriter` grants

reader), which `deployer` can hold safely.

apply (~4 times over the next year). If that becomes annoying, the loosening is to grant `deployer`
`iam.serviceAccountAdmin` + `projectIamAdmin` and move SAs back into `substrate`.

- `config.ts`: `deployers` becomes `["group:it-admin@…"]`; per-user entries go away.
- `docs/manual-setup.md`: new section for the `master@`/GAM steps — create the `it-admin@` group,
  add members, apply `access` once.

### 2. Local tooling

- **`just doctor`** — one preflight: devshell present, active gcloud account, ADC present *and*
  which identity it resolves to, pulumi login, podman socket reachable. Prints the exact command to
  fix whatever's missing. `deploy` and `preview` depend on it, so a bad credential fails in a second
  with an actionable message instead of 90 seconds into an apply with an `oauth2:` error.
- Move both `getClientConfig` calls inside their `docker.Image` resource so an expired token fails
  one resource with a clear message rather than the whole program.
- `just preview`; `just deploy` passes `--yes` through so it works non-interactively; `just ssh` and
  `just logs <service>` (the IAP SSH command was typed 53 times across two sessions).
- **Project-local credentials:** `CLOUDSDK_CONFIG="$PWD/.gcloud"` in `.envrc` (gitignored) so the
  ADC file is per-project instead of one global file shared with personal work. `auth-adc` drops
  persistent `--impersonate-service-account` and logs ADC in as **you** — which is what makes
  deploys work as yourself.
- **Fix the docs** (`README.md:48`, CLAUDE.md): Pulumi and docker authenticate via ADC, not the

- Split `just fmt` (writes) from `just check` (CI, `--fail-on-change`) — 14 of 34 `check` runs in

- Add `.github/dependabot.yml` (npm + github-actions, weekly, grouped).

- Apply the `it-admin@` group binding **additively** first, keeping the existing per-user grants.

- Custom roles are soft-deleted for 7 days and the ID can't be reused in that window, so avoid

- Keep the direct `user:master@` break-glass binding at all times.

## Impact

Deploys run as you, under group membership plus a scoped role, with no standing per-user admin and
no `master@` logins for routine work. Access management becomes "add them to `it-admin@`" — which is
also the onboarding path for a second developer. And the whole class of "opaque failure 90 seconds

- Triggered by the #64 platform bootstrap failure and the #97/#100 people-hub deploys.

This raises an important flag though: the #100 cleanup script that removes non-substrate-labeled containers needs to be narrowed, or it'll wrongly delete legitimate app compose projects — that fix would actively conflict with this design. This is a prerequisite for the next issue: splitting into separate access/infrastructure/people-hub Pulumi projects.

For priority, I'm landing on P2 — there's real friction from having one monolithic stack, but it has a working workaround, even though it's foundational for onboarding a second developer and building app #2. Structurally, `infrastructure` stays untouched to avoid migrating network/SQL/VM/IP/DNS/registry state, a new `access` project comes from #87, and a new Pulumi project lives inside the existing `people-hub` package alongside schema.yaml, taking over just the DirectusSchema and permission rules while the Directus instance and its database stay elsewhere.

The fix is a scoped diff: pull the live snapshot, replace only the app's own collections with what's in schema.yaml, then diff the merged result. Owned collections should be derived directly from schema.yaml rather than a hand-maintained list, which also eliminates the duplicated allCollections list in people-hub.ts that currently exists just for permission rules.

Longer term, I'd want to fan schema.yaml into per-collection resources against the individual endpoints so cross-app deletion becomes structurally impossible, mirroring real Pulumi diff semantics — but that can wait until app #2 actually exists. ## Problem

Changing anything about a running app requires either replacing the VM or SSHing in and doing it by
hand.

The whole compose stack is embedded in the VM's cloud-init `user-data`
(`substrate-bootstrap.ts:38`), and Container-Optimized OS runs cloud-init **only on first boot** —
`compute.ts:74` says so outright: _"Replacing the VM re-runs it; changing it on a running VM does
not."_ So editing `packages/substrate/deploy/docker-compose.yml` produces a Pulumi diff that
changes nothing live. The options are hand-applying over IAP SSH, or forcing a VM replace — which
with `deleteBeforeReplace` means downtime *and* races the Directus dynamic resources against their
180s reachability window.

Measured across the 2026-09-09/10 deploy sessions:

- **53 ×** `gcloud compute ssh … --tunnel-through-iap` to inspect or fix the VM by hand
- **28 ×** `pulumi up`, **29 ×** `pulumi preview`
- **9 ×** `Directus at … did not become reachable within 180000ms`
- **2 ×** `pulumi cancel` to clear a stack lock left by a killed run

It's also the shape of #99: the pre-rename `portal` compose project was never torn down, kept
holding host ports 80/443, and broke the substrate stack's own Caddy — because there was no
mechanism to reconcile what's actually running on the VM against what's declared in git.

## Scope

### 1. Make the bootstrap re-runnable

Rework `bootstrapScript` (`substrate-bootstrap-script.ts`) to be idempotent and safe to re-run,
installed on the VM as a systemd unit rather than a one-shot cloud-init script.

### 2. Let `pulumi up` actually apply it

Apply it from Pulumi via remote exec — `@pulumi/command`'s `remote.Command`, or a `local.Command`
wrapping `gcloud compute ssh --tunnel-through-iap` — with
`triggers: [hash(composeContent), imageUrl]` so a compose or image change reconciles the running
stack with no VM replacement and no downtime.

No new IAM required: `compute.ts:35` already grants deployers `roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor` +
`roles/compute.osLogin`. This would be the first thing to use that access from Pulumi rather than
from a human's terminal.

**This is a real capability change and worth stating plainly:** `pulumi up` gains shell-exec on the
VM. That was proposed and rejected for #99 — correctly, because there it meant building SSH
machinery to self-heal a one-off bootstrap bug. This is different: it's the normal deploy path for
every app change from here on, and it's what makes FreeScout (#67) and Listmonk (#71) deployable at
all without rebuilding the VM each time.

### 3. One compose project per app

Required so each app can own its own deployment (and, later, its own Pulumi project):

- `infrastructure` creates an **external docker network** and runs caddy + oauth2-proxy as its own
  compose project. **Only that project publishes host ports 80/443.**
- Caddy's config becomes `import /etc/caddy/conf.d/*.caddy`.
- Each app ships its own `deploy/docker-compose.yml`, brought up as its own compose project
  (`docker compose -p <app> up -d`) attached to the shared network, **binding no host ports**, plus
  its own `conf.d/<app>.caddy` fragment and a `caddy reload`.

⚠️ **This directly conflicts with the cleanup step added in #100.** `substrate-bootstrap-script.ts`
currently removes any running container whose `com.docker.compose.project` label isn't `substrate` —
under this design that would delete every legitimate app compose project. It must be narrowed to
"remove containers publishing host ports 80/443 that aren't ours" (or dropped in favour of an
explicit known-projects allowlist). The port-collision class that caused #99 is prevented here by
exclusive port ownership, not by the sweep.

### 4. Automate the last manual step

With remote exec available, `docs/manual-setup.md` §6.1's Postgres `GRANT` stops being irreducible —
the VM has a network path to Cloud SQL's private IP, which is the only reason it was manual. Run it
from the VM, idempotently, and delete the manual step from the doc.

### 5. Shorten the reachability wait

Once the apply doesn't complete until the compose project is up, `waitForReachable`'s 180s window
(`directus-client.ts:23`) stops being a race against VM boot. Keep it as a safety net; shorten it.

## Test plan

- Unit tests for the templating and the narrowed cleanup logic, extending
  `packages/infrastructure/test/substrate-bootstrap-script.test.ts`.
- The remote script itself can't be exercised in CI (needs a real VM); verify by hand that a
  compose-only change reconciles with no VM replacement, and that an app project survives a
  substrate re-apply.

## Impact

Editing a compose file becomes one `pulumi up` with no VM replace, no downtime, and no SSH. This is
the single biggest source of friction in the deploy loop, and it's a prerequisite for splitting the
Pulumi program into per-app projects.

## Related

- Blocks the `access` / `infrastructure` / per-app project split (filed separately).
- Must narrow the container-cleanup logic introduced in #100 (fixing #99).
- Removes the last manual step from `docs/manual-setup.md` §6.1.
- Unblocks #67 (FreeScout) and #71 (Listmonk), which each need to deploy to the VM independently.
- `just ssh` / `just logs` land in #87; this makes reaching for them mostly unnecessary.
EOF

## Problem

One Pulumi program (`packages/infrastructure`) holds everything: project IAM, networking, Cloud SQL,
the VM, DNS, the artifact registry, the portal, the Directus instance, **and** the people hub's
Directus schema/roles/permissions. Three consequences, all observed during the #97/#100 deploys:

1. **Different actors are mixed together.** Project-level IAM needs `master@`; everything else
   shouldn't. Because they're in one program, the whole apply gets dragged up to super-admin. (#87
   fixes the IAM half; this issue creates the boundary that keeps it fixed.)
2. **App-layer resources race infrastructure they depend on.** `people-hub.ts` creates Directus
   schema/roles/users over HTTP against a VM the same `pulumi up` is still booting — 9 ×
   `did not become reachable within 180000ms`. `docs/manual-setup.md` §6.2 already concedes _"on a
   truly fresh deploy this is often the second `pulumi up`."_
3. **Every preview touches everything.** 29 previews across two sessions, each diffing Cloud SQL and
   the VM to change a Directus field.

## Scope

Three Pulumi **projects** (each with its own `Pulumi.yaml` and one `prod` stack), wired with
`StackReference`:

| Project | Directory | Contents | Applied by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `access` | `packages/access` (new) | `deployer` custom role, `it-admin@` binding, break-glass grants, **all service accounts**, **all project-level `IAMMember`s** | `master@`, rarely |
| `infrastructure` | `packages/infrastructure` (unchanged) | network + private services connection, Cloud SQL instance, VM + IAP grants, static IP, DNS zones **and records**, artifact registry, shared Google OAuth client, Caddy + oauth2-proxy, portal, **the Directus instance** (compose service, its DB + Postgres role, its secrets, `directus.cycsail.team`), Directus **roles and users** | `it-admin` |
| `people-hub` | `packages/people-hub` (existing — add `Pulumi.yaml` beside `schema.yaml`) | its `schema.yaml` and its **permission rules** only | `it-admin` |

The existing project keeps its name and its state (`ungood/infrastructure/prod`), so network, Cloud
SQL, the VM, the static IP, DNS, and the registry **never move** — no migration risk on anything
expensive or irreplaceable.

### One Directus instance, many app schemas

Directus is shared infrastructure, like Cloud SQL and Caddy. An app project contributes a schema and
the permission rules attaching its collections to platform roles; it does not own the instance.
Consequences:

- **Roles and users live in `infrastructure`**, since they're identity concepts spanning apps — a
  Staff member needs both the people hub and (eventually) the finance app.
- `DirectusPermissionRule` is currently an interface passed *into* `DirectusRole` as
  `permissionRules` (`directus.ts`, `people-hub.ts`). It becomes its own dynamic resource keyed by
  (roleId, collection, action), so an app can attach rules to a role it doesn't own.
- Judgment call to confirm: `Guardian` is arguably people-hub-specific rather than platform-level.
  Starting it in `infrastructure` for consistency with the #65 identity model; easy to flip.
- Applying two app schemas to one instance is **currently unsafe** — see the separate `applySchema`
  bug. That must land before a second app schema exists.

### Cross-project plumbing

- A typed `refs.ts` per project wrapping its `StackReference`, so app code never sprinkles
  string-keyed `getOutput` calls. Roughly 8–12 outputs (SA emails/members, VM name + zone, SQL
  instance name + private IP, docker network name, zone names, registry URL, Directus base URL,
  role IDs).
- Resource-scoped IAM still works unchanged across a boundary — `Secret.grant()` takes a member
  string, so an app granting the substrate SA read on its own secret is identical.
- `enableService` is memoized per-program, so each project enables what it needs. Harmless:
  `disableOnDestroy: false` already makes it idempotent.
- `just deploy` runs the projects in dependency order; `just deploy <project>` for one.

### Two small wins that fall out

- PR #100's `dependsOn: directusAdminBootstrapPassword.version` becomes unnecessary in the app
  project — cross-project ordering ("infrastructure applied first") does that job.
- Keep reading the Directus admin password from Secret Manager directly rather than exporting it as
  a stack output, so the value never lands in a second state file.

## Migration safety

Only the Directus **dynamic** resources move (schema, permission rules) — and those are recreatable
by design. Everything with data or an IP address stays put. Still:

- **Export the Directus database before starting.**
- Use `pulumi state move` if the CLI version supports it; otherwise `stack export` → edit → `import`.
- Run `--target`ed previews and read every diff. **If a preview proposes deleting a `gcp:sql`
  resource, stop** — `database.ts` sets `deletionProtection: true` on data that can't be recreated.
- `access` is nearly migration-free: mostly new resources, plus cheap re-imports.

## Non-goals

- **Not** per-app *stacks* in the environment sense (dev/prod per app) — one `prod` stack each.
- The **portal stays in `infrastructure`**. `portal.ts` is 25 lines: a cookie secret and an A record
  for a static site Caddy already serves. An app earns its own project when it has its own schema,
  state, and lifecycle — Directus/people-hub qualifies, FreeScout (#67) and Listmonk (#71) will, the
  link shortener (#73) probably never will.
- `run-reports-job` stays where it is; it has no substrate coupling and splitting it buys nothing
  today.
- Not renaming `infrastructure` → `substrate`: `packages/substrate` already means the Caddy image
  and compose files, and renaming would move state for no benefit.

## Impact

Schema work — the thing that changes constantly — happens in a project containing **no GCP
resources at all**: no IAM, no networking, no DNS, nothing destructive in scope. That's the
onboarding path for a second developer, and it makes previews narrow and fast.

## Related

- **Depends on** the re-runnable substrate bootstrap (#107) — per-app compose projects are what let
  an app project deploy itself.
- **Depends on** #87 for the `access` project's contents.
- **Blocked by** the `applySchema` cross-app deletion bug (filed separately) before a second app
  schema lands.
- Future seam, not now: once FreeScout and Listmonk land in `infrastructure`, the next natural split
  is "the VM" vs "the services running on it".
EOF

## Problem

`applySchema` (`packages/infrastructure/src/directus-client.ts:88`) posts the **entire** schema
snapshot to Directus's `/schema/diff`. Directus diffs that snapshot against the **whole instance**
and returns everything needed to make the instance match — including **deletions for collections the
snapshot doesn't mention**.

There is one shared Directus instance by design (see #108 — apps contribute schemas, they don't get
their own instance). So as soon as a second app schema exists:

- `people-hub` applies its snapshot → the diff proposes dropping every `finance` collection
- `finance` applies its snapshot → the diff proposes dropping every `people-hub` collection

Each `pulumi up` silently destroys the other app's collections **and their data**. `applySchema`
would report success, because from its perspective the instance now matches the snapshot it sent.

Not currently reachable: `people-hub` is the only app schema today (`people-hub.ts` →
`DirectusSchema("people-hub-schema")`). It becomes live the moment a second one lands — the finance
app that's already being planned around the shared program/session/class vocabulary.

Filed P1 rather than P0 because it cannot fire until a second app schema exists. **Raise to P0 the
moment one is in flight.**

## Verify first

Cheap to confirm before building on the assumption — same throwaway-container approach used to
diagnose #99:

1. `directus/directus:12.3.1` + `postgres:16-alpine`, let it bootstrap
2. create two collections, `a` and `b`
3. `GET /schema/snapshot`, strip `b` from it
4. `POST /schema/diff` with the stripped snapshot
5. check whether the response contains a delete for `b`

If it doesn't behave as described, close this — but the fix below is worth it regardless, since it
also makes each app's schema self-contained.

## Fix

Scope the diff instead of sending a bare snapshot:

1. `GET /schema/snapshot` for the live instance
2. replace **only this app's own collections** with the ones from its `schema.yaml`
3. diff and apply the merged snapshot

Other apps' collections match, so nothing is proposed for deletion; deletions *within* the app's own
namespace still work correctly.

**Derive the owned-collection list from `schema.yaml` itself — never a hand-maintained parallel
list.** A collection missing from that list would be deleted, so drift is a data-loss footgun.
Deriving it also removes an existing duplication: `people-hub.ts`'s `allCollections` array is
maintained by hand today purely to build the Staff permission rules, and can come from the same
place.

## Long-term

When a second app schema actually lands, replace snapshot-apply with per-collection resources —
`DirectusCollection` / `DirectusField` / `DirectusRelation` against `/collections`, `/fields`,
`/relations`, fanned out from the committed `schema.yaml` so it stays the reviewable authoring
format. Cross-app deletion becomes impossible by construction, and previews show real diffs (a
renamed field as a replace) instead of the whole schema being one opaque resource. The dynamic
resource pattern and the testable client boundary already exist in `directus.ts` /
`directus-client.ts`, so it's more typing than difficulty.

Leave a comment at `applySchema` explaining why the scoped diff exists, so app #2 doesn't get built
on the unsafe version.

## Test plan

Regression test in `packages/infrastructure/test/` mocking `fetch` at the client boundary (matching
the existing `directus-client.test.ts` pattern):

- a merged snapshot **preserves** collections outside the app's namespace
- it still **deletes** a collection removed from the app's own `schema.yaml`
- the owned-collection set is derived from the schema, not passed in separately

## Related

- Blocks the per-app split (#108) from safely supporting a second app schema.
- Same code path as #101 (the `directus:` version field drifting from the pinned image) — worth
  re-reading `applySchema` as a whole while in there.
- Context: #69 (people hub), and the finance app that motivated the shared program/session/class
  terminology.
EOF

Base directory for this skill: /Users/ungood/workspaces/personal/isthmia/.claude/skills/work-backlog

# Work the Backlog

Top-level orchestrator that turns the open issue backlog into merged PRs. It does **not** write code itself — it triages, decides what's next, and delegates each issue to a sub-agent running the `work-issue` skill. It owns the long waits (plan approval, human merge) that a one-shot sub-agent can't sit through.

## Constraints

- **One issue in flight at a time.** Never start a second issue until the current one's PR is merged or closed. Exactly one active branch/PR — no parallel work (for now).
- **Never merge.** Humans merge PRs manually; that's the approval (see `work-issue`).

## Workflow

### 1. Triage first

Run the `triage` skill so every open issue has a type + priority label, duplicates are resolved, and unclear issues are flagged. A clean, prioritized backlog is the input to selection.

### 2. Build the work queue

Order actionable issues by priority (`P0` → `P3`, then oldest first). **Exclude** issues that aren't ready:

- Blocked on a human: `plan-review` label present, or the body says it depends on another issue ("land #X first").
- Ambiguous / needs a decision (flagged during triage).
- Already in progress: an open PR or branch already references it.

Show the user the resulting queue and the issue you intend to start. Proceed with the top item unless it needs a decision only the user can make — then ask first.

### 3. Delegate one issue to a sub-agent

content.content:
## Proposed plan

### Verification (done)

Reproduced with a throwaway `directus/directus:12.3.1` + `postgres:16-alpine` pair (removed after):
created collections `a` and `b`, took `GET /schema/snapshot`, stripped `b` out, and `POST`ed the
result to `/schema/diff`. The response proposed a `D` (delete) entry for collection `b`:

```json
{"kind": "D", "lhs": {"collection": "b", "meta": {...}, "schema": {"name": "b"}}}
```

Went one step further and fed that diff to `/schema/apply`: collection `b` was actually dropped,
`a` was untouched. Confirms the issue exactly as described — a snapshot that omits a collection is
read by Directus as "delete this," not "I have no opinion about this."

### Fix

In `packages/infrastructure/src/directus-client.ts`:

- Add a minimal typed shape for what we touch in a snapshot:
  ```ts
  interface DirectusSnapshot {
    version: number;
    directus: string;
    vendor: string;
    collections: { collection: string }[];
    fields: { collection: string }[];
    relations: { collection: string }[];
  }
  ```
- `getSnapshot(baseUrl, token)` — `GET /schema/snapshot`, returns `DirectusSnapshot`.
- `collectionsInSchema(schema: unknown): string[]` (exported) — `(schema as DirectusSnapshot).collections.map(c => c.collection)`.
  This is the single derivation point: `applySchema` uses it internally for the owned-collection
  set, and `people-hub.ts` uses it externally to replace its hand-maintained `allCollections` array
  (built from the same `schema.yaml` it already loads).
- `scopeSnapshot(live: DirectusSnapshot, appSchema: DirectusSnapshot, owned: Set<string>): DirectusSnapshot`
  — starts from `live`, then for `collections`/`fields`/`relations` drops any entry whose
  `collection` is in `owned` and appends `appSchema`'s own entries for those arrays. Relations are
  keyed by their owning (`many`) side's `collection` field, consistent with collections/fields, so a
  relation this app doesn't own is never touched.
- `applySchema(baseUrl, token, schema)` changes internally (signature unchanged) to:
  1. `getSnapshot` (live)
  2. `collectionsInSchema(schema)` → owned set
  3. `scopeSnapshot(live, schema, owned)` → merged snapshot
  4. diff/apply/re-diff against the **merged** snapshot instead of the bare `schema`
- Leave a comment at `applySchema` explaining why the scoped diff exists (per the issue), so app #2
  doesn't get built on the unsafe version.

In `packages/infrastructure/src/people-hub.ts`:

- Replace the hand-maintained `allCollections` array with `collectionsInSchema(schema)`.

### Tests (`packages/infrastructure/test/directus-client.test.ts`)

Existing tests mock `fetch` starting at `POST /schema/diff`; they need an added leading
`GET /schema/snapshot` mock response now that `applySchema` fetches the live snapshot first. New
cases per the issue's test plan:

- a merged snapshot **preserves** a collection outside the app's namespace (present in the mocked
  live snapshot, absent from the app schema) — assert it's still in the body posted to
  `/schema/diff`/passed through untouched.
- it still **deletes** a collection removed from the app's own `schema.yaml` (present in live under
  the app's prior schema, absent from the new app schema) — assert it's dropped from the merged
  snapshot handed to the diff.
- the owned-collection set comes from `schema` alone — `collectionsInSchema` tested directly against
  a snapshot-shaped object, and `applySchema` takes no separate owned-collections parameter.

### Explicitly out of scope

Per the issue: no per-collection `DirectusCollection`/`DirectusField`/`DirectusRelation` fan-out.
That's the long-term follow-up already captured in the issue body — not filing a separate issue for
it.

### Open question

None — the issue's "Fix" section already specifies the approach; this plan is mostly nailing down
the exact function boundary (`collectionsInSchema`/`scopeSnapshot`/`getSnapshot` in
`directus-client.ts`) so the merge logic is unit-testable at the same `fetch`-mocking boundary as
today.

The agent came back at the plan gate — it did run the experiment rather than assuming, and went a step further than I asked.

**Premise confirmed.** Against a throwaway `12.3.1` + Postgres pair: created collections `a` and `b`, took a snapshot, stripped `b`, posted to `/schema/diff` → got back `{"kind": "D", "lhs": {"collection": "b", …}}`. It then fed that diff to `/schema/apply` and **`b` was actually dropped** while `a` survived. So #109 is real and reproducible with a two-collection case, not a theoretical hazard. Containers torn down after.

The [plan](https://github.com/cyc-seattle/isthmia/issues/109#issuecomment-5623946114) is mostly good — `getSnapshot` / `collectionsInSchema` / `scopeSnapshot` in `directus-client.ts`, merging `collections`, `fields`, **and** `relations` (I was worried it would only merge collections and leave other apps' fields proposed for deletion; it doesn't), and replacing `people-hub.ts`'s hand-maintained `allCollections`.

**But it contains a contradiction that needs resolving before it's implemented.**

The owned set is derived from the *new* `schema.yaml`, and `scopeSnapshot` drops from live only what's in that set. Trace a collection you delete from `schema.yaml`:

- `owned` no longer contains `people`
- so `people` is **not** dropped from the live half
- and it's **not** re-added from the app schema
- merged snapshot still contains `people` → diff sees no change → never deleted

So removing a collection from `schema.yaml` silently does nothing. That directly contradicts the plan's own second test case ("it still deletes a collection removed from the app's own `schema.yaml`"), which would fail as specified. This is the tension I flagged when we designed it and didn't fully resolve: **you can't derive the owned set from the desired schema alone and still support deletion.**

Three ways out:

1. **Track the previously-owned set in the dynamic resource's state.** `DirectusSchema` is already a Pulumi dynamic resource, so its provider gets `olds` on update. Store `ownedCollections` in the output state and use `olds ∪ news` as the drop set. Correct, cheap, fits the existing architecture — `applySchema`'s signature changes, which the plan wanted to avoid, but that's a small price.
2. **Accept that deletion is never automatic.** Removing a collection from `schema.yaml` leaves it in place; dropping it is a deliberate manual action. Defensible for a data-bearing CRM, and arguably safer. Requires fixing the test expectation, not the code.
3. Per-app collection name prefixes. More invasive, and it'd churn your existing schema.

I'd go with **1**, with **2** as a reasonable answer if you'd rather no automated path can ever drop a collection holding real people data.

One side effect worth knowing either way: because the merged snapshot inherits `version`/`directus`/`vendor` from the **live** instance, the version check that produced #101 can never fire again. I think that's fine — it was only ever metadata — but it does quietly retire a guardrail.

The `plan-review` label is yours to remove; I won't approve on your behalf. Tell me which option you want and I'll send the revision back to the same agent (it keeps its context, including the live repro it already built).

entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will process your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

content.text:
Verified independently — I read the merged diff rather than trusting the report. It's sound.

**All five amendment items are present and correctly implemented:**

- `scopeSnapshot` spreads `...live` first, so `version`/`directus`/`vendor` come from the live instance (item 5), and the doc comment says so explicitly
- a collection dropped from `schema.yaml` isn't in `owned`, so it survives from the live half — documented as deliberate in both `scopeSnapshot` and `applySchema` (items 1, 2)
- `hasCollectionDelete` is checked **before** `/schema/apply`, not after — correct placement (item 3)
- the collection-vs-field boundary is documented precisely, including that field removals drop columns and data (item 4)

**On the two out-of-plan fixes, both are justified:**

The `path === undefined` refinement in `hasCollectionDelete` matches the actual diff shape from the live repro earlier in this session — `{"kind":"D","lhs":{"collection":"b",…}}` carried no `path`. And its failure modes are benign in both directions: a false negative just falls back to the scoping (which is the real protection), a false positive blocks a deploy loudly. The `schemaDiff` 204 fix is genuinely required — without it `applySchema` crashes on the in-sync case, which the scoping makes the *common* case. Both are well-commented as to why they're there.

**I checked the one thing that could have been a silent security change:** `allCollections` is now derived from `schema.yaml` instead of hand-maintained, which drives the Staff role's CRUD permissions. The derived set is exactly the same 11 collections as the old array — no permission expansion. Only the *order* differs (alphabetical from YAML), so expect a cosmetic update to `people-hub-staff` in the next preview.

Three things to know, none blocking:

1. **Nothing has run against production.** All verification was local containers. `crm.cycsail.team` already has this schema applied, so the first real `pulumi up` should hit the in-sync path and no-op — but that apply is the first live exercise of both new code paths. Worth watching it rather than running it unattended.
2. `collectionsInSchema` does an unchecked `as DirectusSnapshot` cast, so a malformed `schema.yaml` would crash at module scope in `people-hub.ts` with a bare `TypeError` during preview. Minor, but a validation guard would give a better error.
3. `hasCollectionDelete` depends on an undocumented `deep-diff` shape detail. Fine as defense-in-depth, but it could quietly become a no-op across a Directus upgrade — the scoping would still protect you.

The verification-against-real-containers claims are the agent's; I confirmed the implementation and CI, not those runs.

[PR #110](https://github.com/cyc-seattle/isthmia/pull/110) is green, `CLEAN`, reviewer requested — yours to merge. Once you do, I'll clean up the branch and dispatch #107.

#109 is closed with its branch deleted, now on main at be46e40c. Moving to dispatch #107, I need to set clear guardrails in the prompt so the agent doesn't run `pulumi up` or `just deploy` against production — no live infra changes allowed, and I'm leaning toward disallowing applies entirely given potential credential issues with ADC and a known module-scope bug in getClientConfig.

This will almost certainly require plan approval given the scope, and the #100 cleanup conflict needs explicit attention. The agent can verify locally by testing shell logic against docker containers, following the #99/#100 precedent, and unit-testing the templating.

The issue has five scope items and feels large — idempotent bootstrap with a systemd unit, Pulumi remote-exec with triggers, and per-app compose projects touching Caddy config among them. I'm debating whether to have the agent propose splitting this into stages within its plan rather than trying to land it all in one PR, since keeping to "one issue in flight" while still being honest about the size seems like the right balance to bring to the user.

Looking closer, items 1-4 are really coupled together (you can't do the per-app compose work without the bootstrap and remote-exec pieces), while automating the GRANT is separable and shortening waitForReachable is trivial — so I want the agent's plan to flag if it thinks this needs multiple PRs rather than deciding that unilaterally. There's also a wrinkle around where Directus lives: since it's shared infrastructure per #108, it might stay in the substrate compose project alongside caddy and oauth2-proxy, which raises the question of what the per-app compose projects are actually meant to isolate.

Under #107 the substrate project would house caddy, oauth2-proxy, and Directus, while per-app projects only apply to future apps like FreeScout and Listmonk — meaning the new per-app mechanism has no real consumer today. Thinking it through more, I lean toward actually moving Directus into its own compose project as the first proof of the new mechanism, even though its Pulumi resources still live in infrastructure, rather than leaving it in the substrate project with nothing demonstrating the pattern.

A compose project boundary doesn't need to match a Pulumi project boundary — infrastructure can still deploy both the substrate compose project and a separate directus compose project, which is a subtlety worth spelling out explicitly since it could otherwise confuse things. I want to flag this as a deliberate design choice to the user rather than silently deciding it myself.

I should have the agent propose this in the plan and note it's my suggestion so the user can veto during plan review, and point them to the earlier commit that cleaned up the bootstrap script so they understand what needs narrowing. Then I'll dispatch this with the sonnet model.

Good — that unblocks #87 when it reaches the front. One catch specific to your setup that's worth getting right at creation time.

**`ungood@onetrue.name` is external to `cyccommunitysailing.org`.** So the group can't be locked with `allowexternalmembers false` — you'd be unable to add yourself, which is the whole point. That makes the safe configuration:

- `allowexternalmembers true` (required for your account)
- but `whocanjoin invited_can_join` — never self-service, or anyone who discovers the address could grant themselves deploy rights
- restrict who can add members to owners/managers only
- membership visible to members, not the org

That combination is what keeps an externally-open group from becoming a privilege-escalation path once IAM is bound to it. This is the same cross-domain wrinkle you already hit with `all@` and oauth2-proxy.

The devshell has `gam` with `GAM_ADMIN_USER=master@cyccommunitysailing.org` already set, so roughly:

```sh
gam create group it-admin@cyccommunitysailing.org \
  name "IT Admin" \
  description "Platform deploy access (bound to the deployer IAM role) - see cyc-seattle/isthmia#87"
gam update group it-admin@cyccommunitysailing.org \
  whocanjoin invited_can_join \
  allowexternalmembers true \
  whocaninvite all_managers_can_invite \
  whocanviewmembership all_members_can_view
gam update group it-admin@cyccommunitysailing.org add member ungood@onetrue.name
gam info group it-admin@cyccommunitysailing.org
```
